{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2022}}
The '''Population Investigation Committee''' is a United Kingdom social research group founded in 1936 by the council of the [[British Eugenics Society]].<ref name=":5" />

Its original members included [[David Glass (sociologist)|David V. Glass]], [[Griselda Rowntree]] and [[James W. B. Douglas|J.W.B. Douglas]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Pearson |first=Helen |title=The life project : the extraordinary story of our ordinary lives |date=2017 |isbn=978-0-14-197661-7 |location=London |oclc=990398191}}</ref> Since the second world war it has been housed at the [[London School of Economics]] (LSE).<ref name=":0" />

The PIC founded a journal, ''[[Population Studies (journal)|Population Studies]]'' and also a Scholarship Fund for UK students studying for master's degrees in demography.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Population Investigation Committee on JSTOR |url=https://www.jstor.org/publisher/pic |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.jstor.org}}</ref>

== Formation ==
The origins of the PIC lie in an annual lecture of the Eugenics Society. On 16 February 1935, the Society's [[Francis Galton|Galton]] Lecture was delivered by [[Alexander Carr-Saunders|Sir Alexander Carr-Saunders]], Charles Booth Chair of Social Science at the [[University of Liverpool]], and Chairman of the Eugenics Society's [[Eugenics|Positive Eugenics]] Committee. Entitled "Eugenics in the Light of Population Trends", Carr-Saunders's lecture drew attention to the falling birth rate in Britain and his fears for what this meant for British society.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Grebenik |first=E. |date=1991 |title=Demographic Research in Britain 1936-1986 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2175057 |journal=Population Studies |volume=45 |pages=3–30 |jstor=2175057 |issn=0032-4728}}</ref>

Carr-Saunders argued for a more structured approach to the topic of population and the creation of a "coherent population policy".<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Carr-Saunders |first=A. M. |date=1935 |title=Eugenics in the light of population trends |journal=The Eugenics Review |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=11–20 |doi= |issn= |pmc=2985420 |pmid=21260157}}</ref> It was towards these ends that the Council of the Eugenics Society formed a research body – the Population Investigation Committee - in 1936.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sear |first=Rebecca |date=2021-12-15 |title=Demography and the rise, apparent fall, and resurgence of eugenics |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00324728.2021.2009013 |journal=Population Studies |language=en |volume=75 |issue=sup1 |pages=201–220 |doi=10.1080/00324728.2021.2009013 |issn=0032-4728}}</ref>

At the first meeting of the PIC on 15 June 1936, Carr-Saunders was elected Chairman of the committee, [[Carlos Blacker|C.P. Blacker]] the General Secretary, and [[David Glass (sociologist)|David Glass]] the Research Secretary. It was also resolved that the PIC would be an independent organisation to the Eugenics Society (and to other organisations who had appointed representatives to the PIC).<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Science |first=London School of Economics and Political |title=The history of the PIC and the archives |url=https://www.lse.ac.uk/international-development/research/population-investigation-committee/history.aspx |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=London School of Economics and Political Science |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Despite Carr-Saunders original call for a "coherent population policy", the PIC's originating remit was towards research, not in formulating policy. As such, the PIC played a major role in a number of national surveys which sought to investigate the "medical, economic and social factors affecting changes in the population".<ref name=":4" />

== Research ==
The PIC has been involved in a number of social science research projects, the most notable were the [[National Survey of Health and Development]] and the [[Lothian birth-cohort studies|Scottish Mental Survey of 1947]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Ramsden |first=Edmund |date=2014 |title=Surveying the meritocracy: The problems of intelligence and mobility in the studies of the Population Investigation Committee |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1369848614000533 |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part C: Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences |language=en |volume=47 |pages=130–141 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsc.2014.05.013|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The [[National Survey of Health and Development]] developed from a Maternity Inquiry established in 1946 through a collaboration of the PIC with the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=Katherine |date=2022-10-22 |title=Claims to (S)expertise in the British Sex Survey, c. 1960s–1990s |url=https://academic.oup.com/shm/advance-article/doi/10.1093/shm/hkac042/6769944 |journal=Social History of Medicine |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=660–680 |language=en |doi=10.1093/shm/hkac042 |issn=0951-631X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The [[Lothian birth-cohort studies|Scottish Mental Survey of 1947]] was carried out by the PIC in cooperation with the [[Scottish Council for Research in Education]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deary |first=Ian J. |date=2013 |title=An intelligent Scotland: Professor Sir godfrey Thomson and the Scottish Mental Surveys of 1932 and 1947 |url=http://www.britac.ac.uk/journal/1/deary.cfm |journal=Journal of the British Academy |volume=1 |pages=95–131 |doi=10.5871/jba/001.095|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Other research activities of the PIC included inquiries and surveys into fertility and birth control; marriage and divorce and the British Peerage.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=CPC - Latest News - The Population Investigation Committee: its history and influence over the last 75 years |url=https://www.cpc.ac.uk/news/latest_news/?action=story&id=70 |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.cpc.ac.uk}}</ref>

== ''Population Studies'' ==
The PIC's journal, ''Population Studies'', was established in 1947. It was the first English-language journal "exclusively concerned with [[demography]]".<ref name=":4" />  ''Population Studies'' was also the place of publication for much of the research carried out by the PIC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Population Studies {{!}} JSTOR |url=https://www.jstor.org/journal/popustud |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.jstor.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Later years ==
It has been suggested that the research outputs of the PIC slowed down after the death of its then Chairman David Glass in 1978.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Population Investigation Committee |url=https://wellcomecollection.org/works/csfdcepz |access-date=2022-06-01 |website=Wellcome Collection |language=en}}</ref>

The work of the PIC remains centred around ''Population Studies'' even if since 2002 the journal has been published externally to the PIC.  The PIC also retains interests in the postgraduate teaching of demography - it established a training programme in demography at the LSE in 1965<ref>{{Cite book |last=Langford |first=C.M. |title=The Population Investigation Committee |date=1988 |publisher=Population Investigation Committee at the London School of Economics |isbn=978-0-905804-01-9 |pages=19 |language=English |oclc=21597351}}</ref> - and in recent years has maintained a Scholarship Fund (drawn from profits of ''Population Studies'') for the support of UK masters students studying demography.<ref name=":4" />

== Chairmen ==
The Chairmen of the PIC have been:<ref name=":2" />

[[Alexander Carr-Saunders|Sir Alexander Carr-Saunders]] (1936-1958)

[[David Glass (sociologist)|David Glass]] (1958-1978)

[[Ralph Dahrendorf|Prof. Ralph Dahrendorf]] (1978-1984)

[[Tony Wrigley|Prof. Sir Tony Wrigley]] (1984-1991)

Prof. John Hobcraft (1991-2003)

Prof. John Cleland (2003- )
